[assistant] The one architectural change that would make HyperSnatch **dramatically faster** is this: # Move to an Event-Sourced Temporal Core Right now, most systems like this end up slow because they keep recomputing giant graph state over and over. That’s the wrong center of gravity. Instead of treating the **graph as the source of truth**, treat the **event log as the source of truth**. --- ## What that means Every meaningful change becomes an append-only event: ```text timestamp event_type entity_id related_entity_id weight source metadata ``` Examples: ```text domain_registered ip_linked provider_changed narrative_amplified operator_pattern_detected confidence_adjusted ``` Then HyperSnatch does this: ```text raw events ↓ append-only event store ↓ materialized views ↓ graph / heatmap / replay / forecast / copilot ``` That changes everything. --- # Why this makes it 10× faster ## 1. You stop rebuilding the whole graph Most slow systems do this: - ingest data - rebuild graph - rerun scoring - rerender everything That burns time and memory. With an event-sourced core, you only process **new deltas**. --- ## 2. Replay becomes almost free You want the Time Machine engine? This is how you get it. If history is stored as ordered events, replay is just: ```text reconstruct state at T ``` or ```text play events from T1 to T2 ``` That is much cleaner than trying to reverse-engineer time from a static graph snapshot. --- ## 3. Counterfactuals get cheaper Instead of cloning huge graph state, you can do: - base event stream - exclude selected events - re-materialize affected subgraph That’s much lighter than recomputing the universe. --- ## 4. Provenance becomes native Because every edge and score came from events, you can answer: - where did this come from? - when did it enter the system? - what changed it? - what evidence raised confidence? That makes provenance, XAI, and audit trails much easier. --- # The key architectural pattern You want **three layers**. ## Layer 1: Immutable Event Store The permanent truth. ```text /events 2026-01-01-0001.json 2026-01-01-0002.json ``` Could be SQLite, DuckDB, Parquet, JSONL, or a local append-only log. --- ## Layer 2: Materialized State Views Fast derived views for different tasks. Examples: - current graph view - temporal graph slices - operator profile cache - provenance index - heatmap cluster table - forecast input table These are disposable and rebuildable. --- ## Layer 3: Analyst Surfaces The UI doesn’t query raw events directly unless needed. It queries optimized views: - graph explorer - replay engine - challenge mode - command console That keeps the frontend fast. --- # What to cache If you want scale, cache these aggressively: ## Hot caches - neighborhood expansion - cluster density - entity timeline - attribution score breakdown - explanation trees ## Warm caches - operator behavior profiles - propagation chains - forecast feature vectors ## Cold storage - raw events - archived investigations - old provenance bundles --- # The real performance trick Don’t recompute globally. Use **incremental subgraph invalidation**. When a new event lands: 1. identify affected entities 2. identify affected edges 3. invalidate only related caches 4. recompute local views So if one node changes, you don’t touch 500,000 unrelated ones. That’s how serious systems stay fast. --- # Best storage model for HyperSnatch For an offline-first tool, I’d structure it like this: ## Primary store **DuckDB or SQLite** - local - simple - fast enough - portable ## Event archive **JSONL or Parquet** - append-only - easy export - easy audit ## Search / indexing - entity index - time index - provenance index - relationship index This gives you: - reproducibility - offline portability - analytics speed - exportability --- # How the engines would change ## Graph Engine Stops owning truth. It becomes a derived view generator. ## Replay Engine Reads event windows and rebuilds state per time slice. ## Counterfactual Engine Masks or mutates event subsets, then regenerates affected outputs. ## XAI Explains which event chains produced which score. ## Forecast Engine Consumes temporal sequences directly instead of inferring them from static snapshots. That is a massive upgrade. --- # What this looks like in practice Instead of storing: ```text entity A linked to entity B with score 0.8 ``` store: ```text 2026-02-01: ip_observed 2026-02-03: same_provider_detected 2026-02-05: shared_tls_fingerprint 2026-02-06: confidence_adjusted +0.2 2026-02-07: analyst_confirmed linkage ``` Then the current graph edge is just the present interpretation of those events. That’s much more powerful. --- # Why this matters strategically This single change gives you: - speed - replay - provenance - better counterfactuals - better forecasting - better audits - easier long-term maintenance It’s not just optimization. It’s the right backbone. --- # If I were doing HyperSnatch v2 architecture I’d define: ```text 1. Event Kernel 2. Derived Graph Layer 3. Temporal Analytics Layer 4. Analyst Interaction Layer 5. Release / Audit Layer ``` And I’d make the event kernel the constitutional center of the whole system. --- # Brutal truth A lot of investigation tools look impressive until datasets get big. Then they choke because they were built around **snapshot graphs**, not **temporal event streams**. If HyperSnatch ever needed to handle serious scale, this is the change that would matter most.
